passage:
Sunday night
First real fight with Adil. Not a sulky one, a real one.
It was about his parents. He'd told them we'd come for lunch every Sunday "from now on", without asking me. I said I also need Sundays for my own family and, honestly, for sleep. He said, "But that's how it's always been in our house." I said, "It's not only your house any more."
He went quiet and walked to the window. I thought, here we go, the silent treatment. But after a few minutes he came back and said, "You're right that I should have asked. I'm upset, but I'm not going anywhere. Can we work out a schedule?"
I'd braced for him to storm off. Instead he stayed in the room while being angry. Nandini always says the first fight tells you more than the first date. I think she's right.
Farida

qa.q: What had Adil told his parents without asking?
qa.a: Adil had told them they'd come for lunch every Sunday 'from now on'.

qa.q: What did Farida expect when Adil walked to the window, and how did that change?
qa.a: Farida braced for the silent treatment, then felt reassured when Adil came back, admitted he should have asked and stayed in the conversation.

qa.q: What did Adil's response show that matters for the future?
qa.a: He could be upset and still stay, own his part and move to problem-solving, which suggests they can handle later disagreements together.

qa.q: How might Adil's parents experience the new schedule talk?
qa.a: Adil's parents may feel disappointed at fewer Sunday lunches, since weekly lunches are how it has always been in their house.

grounding: Shows a couple's first real disagreement over time with parents, where how each behaves reveals more about the future than the early months.

passage:
Saturday, 11 p.m.

First real fight with Rukmini today. Not a bicker. A fight.

It started with her sister's wedding. Her family wants us to split the cost of the sangeet decorations since "you two are practically engaged." I said we should talk about it first. She said I was being cheap. I said I wasn't cheap, I just didn't want to be told what to spend by her mother.

Then it got bigger. She said I never want to spend on her family but I spent on my cousin's trip without asking. That landed. She wasn't wrong.

We both went quiet. She left early.

What's bothering me isn't the money. It's how quickly I got defensive. And how she brought up something from months ago. If this is how we fight now, what happens in ten years?

I'll call her tomorrow. Not to win. To listen.

— Sachin

qa.q: What did Rukmini's family want them to split the cost of?
qa.a: The sangeet decorations.

qa.q: What worries Sachin most after the fight?
qa.a: Sachin feels uneasy and worried, less about the money than about how quickly the defensiveness came and what that says about their future.

qa.q: What could Sachin try when he calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Sachin could admit being defensive, listen to Rukmini's side, and suggest they agree together how to handle family expenses.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt when she left early?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and frustrated, feeling that Sachin doesn't value her family and remembering the cousin's trip.

grounding: Sachin's diary shows the first real fight with Rukmini over family expenses, revealing different expectations and how each handles disagreement.

passage:
Farida and Yusuf were to be married in the winter, and everyone in their kasba near Bhopal agreed it was a good match.

Then Farida was selected for the district health programme. It meant travelling to villages three weeks a month.

She told Yusuf on the bench outside the post office, expecting him to be proud. He was quiet for a long time.

"Three weeks?" he said. "Who will be at home?"

"We will be at home. One week a month. Then we'll see."

"My mother expected..."

"Your mother expected. What do you expect?"

He didn't answer. She felt her face go hot. She had assumed they wanted the same things.

Later, at the tailoring shop, her friend Damini listened and said, "Better you know now how he fights than after the wedding."

Farida thought about that all evening. It wasn't the travel she was worried about. It was that silence.

qa.q: How many weeks a month would the programme require Farida to travel?
qa.a: Three weeks a month.

qa.q: What worries Farida most after the talk with Yusuf?
qa.a: She feels worried and let down, not so much about the travel as about Yusuf's silence and what it says about how they handle disagreement.

qa.q: What could Farida and Yusuf do next?
qa.a: Have an open conversation about what each of them expects from marriage and work, instead of leaving it to his mother's expectations or to silence.

qa.q: How might Yusuf be feeling during his long silence?
qa.a: He may be torn and anxious, caught between his mother's expectations and wanting to support Farida.

grounding: Farida's selection for a travelling job causes the first real disagreement with Yusuf, revealing different expectations and how each behaves in conflict.

passage:
The argument started over a calendar. Rafael had written "Mãe, lunch" on every Sunday until December, the way it had always been in his family. Liam saw it on the fridge of their small Lisbon flat and went quiet.
"Every Sunday?"
"It's lunch. It's family."
"It's the only day we both have off."
Rafael felt his face go hot. He had expected Liam to love those loud, crowded tables. Instead Liam said, carefully, "I like your mum. I just thought we'd decide our weekends together."
Rafael wanted to slam the cupboard. He didn't. He sat down, rubbed his eyes and said, "I didn't even know that was a question for us."
Liam half smiled. "Maybe that's the real question."
They didn't settle it that night, but neither of them left the table, and Rafael noticed that mattered more to him than winning.

qa.q: What had Rafael written on every Sunday until December?
qa.a: He had written "Mãe, lunch" on every Sunday until December.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when Liam questioned the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, with his face going hot and an urge to slam the cupboard, because he had expected Liam to love those family lunches.

qa.q: What did Rafael choose at the turning point, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He sat down instead of slamming the cupboard and admitted he hadn't seen weekends as a shared decision, which kept the talk open for another day.

qa.q: How does Liam see the calendar on the fridge?
qa.a: To Liam it looks as if their only shared day off was decided without him, so he wants a say, not a rejection of Rafael's family.

grounding: Shows a couple's first real disagreement, over time with family, revealing different expectations and how each behaves under strain.
